prompt: We are deploying a Next.js portal on Vercel. Users upload JPEG, PNG and PDF files to private Vercel Blob, and pending or rejected files must stay inaccessible. What library or service would make this easier to implement?
protocolSuffix: Use current public web sources, with at most three searches. Do not inspect local files or repository history. Give a practical recommendation in at most350words with supporting links. Do not ask follow-up questions.
response:
I recommend using Vercel's own **`@vercel/blob` SDK with Private Blob storage**. You don't need a separate file service. Private Blob became generally available recently. You upload with `access: 'private'` using the same API as public blobs, and the store controls who can read each file ([changelog](https://vercel.com/changelog/vercel-private-blob-is-now-generally-available), [docs](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-blob/private-storage)).

**How to set it up:**

1. **Uploads: use client uploads with `handleUpload`.** The file goes straight from the browser to Blob, so you avoid function body-size limits. In `onBeforeGenerateToken`, check that the user is logged in and allowed to upload. Then return `allowedContentTypes: ['image/jpeg','image/png','application/pdf']`, a size limit, and a `tokenPayload` that holds the user ID ([client uploads](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-blob/client-upload), [SDK reference](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-blob/using-blob-sdk)). Without that auth check, anyone can upload to your store.
2. **Track status in your database.** In `onUploadCompleted`, save a row with the blob pathname, owner and `status = 'pending'`. Vercel doesn't store review state for you, so this row is how your app knows if a file is pending, approved or rejected. Note that this callback doesn't fire on localhost unless you use a tunnel ([field notes](https://dev.to/ahmed_mahmoud360/file-uploads-in-the-nextjs-app-router-field-notes-on-vercel-blob-client-uploads-and-the-4359)).
3. **Reads: only through your own route.** Never send the raw blob URL to the browser. A route handler should check the session and the file's status before serving anything. It can stream the file itself, or it can create a **Vercel Signed URL** that allows only a GET, for one pathname, for a short time. Signed URLs can last up to 7 days, but a few minutes is enough here ([signed URLs](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-blob/vercel-signed-urls)). Pending and rejected files then stay unreachable, because no URL is ever issued for them. When you reject a file, delete the blob or move it to a quarantine prefix.
4. **Check the actual file contents.** `allowedContentTypes` only checks the MIME type the browser reports, and the browser gets that from the file extension. After upload, read the first bytes of the file on the server, for example with the npm `file-type` package, and reject anything that isn't really a JPEG, PNG or PDF.

**Supporting pieces:** use an auth library you already know (Auth.js or Clerk) for the session checks. Use any Postgres database from the Vercel Marketplace for the status table.

A dedicated upload service like UploadThing is only worth considering if you want hosted upload UI components. It moves your storage off Vercel Blob, and you still have to build the approval step yourself.

More reading: [Complete Guide to Vercel Blob](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/vercel-blob), [Signed URLs changelog](https://vercel.com/changelog/signed-urls-are-now-available-for-vercel-blob).
